Our national education reform agenda under the Nigeria 
Education Sector Reform Initiative (NESRI) is driven by the 
overarching vision to improve learning outcomes and 
empower young people with knowledge, skills and competencies for 
national relevance and global competitiveness. A strategic process 
for achieving this is the overhaul of the school curriculum, as 
enunciated in the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Ahmed 
Tinubu, GCFR, which identified, as a key priority area, the 
development and implementation of a modern standard curriculum 
for the Nigerian education sector. The substance of the agenda was 
given impetus in the Ministerial Deliverables for the Federal Ministry 
of Education, which mandates, among others, a rapid review of the 
educational curriculum across all levels of education to align with 
skills needed in the labour market.
In our quest to achieve this lofty vision, we activated a strategic 
framework for the review, realignment and refocusing of all school 
curricula for functionality and relevance. The plan is to make our 
learners relevant and properly cultivated to contribute effectively to 
societal development, leveraging the right skill set. The above 
underscores the need for us to move from the knowledge-based 
curriculum, which hitherto has dominated our educational 
landscape, to the competency and outcome-based curriculum 
framework with a focus on developing and deepening, in the 
recipients, critical skills for efficient performance in the world of work 
and productive engagement in the ever-changing society. 
Committed to this dream, we have been able to achieve a complete 
reform of the basic education curriculum, aligning it to the national 
developmental agenda and global standards. Logically, the next step 
is the review and remodelling of the senior secondary education 
curriculum to achieve proper linkage with the basic education 
learning contents, as well as expand to learning experiences of a 
higher domain that match their cognitive maturity and societal 
expectations. Thus, the revised senior secondary education 
curriculum is not only competency-based but highly skill-oriented to 
produce citizens with the requisite skills for job creation and wealth 
generation. It has also fully embedded our cherished values, history 
and heritage to ensure that the learners are imbued with qualities 
that are fundamental for building a peaceful and democratic society 
of choice. Furthermore, the curriculum has been designed to expose 
learners to the 21st-century skills for functionality in all spheres of 
human endeavour within and outside the shores of Nigeria. These 
features make the curriculum unique and appropriate to our current 
needs as a nation. 
We wish to state that the development of the curriculum followed 
various stages, best practices, and broadened engagement of a 
range of stakeholders, students, parents, education administrators, 
experts and professional bodies, and development partners. We 
commend the efforts of the Nigerian Educational Research and 
Development Council (NERDC) for the excellent coordination of the 
processes and technical inputs in the design of this new curriculum. 
We also commend all the critical stakeholders, members of the 
academia, teachers, community leaders, policy makers, parents and 
learners who participated at various stages of the development 
process.
 
We wish to reiterate our commitment to the successful 
implementation of the revised curriculum through extensive teacher 
training and orientation, provision of necessary resources, and 
deployment of competent school quality assurance officers. 
Additionally, we will sustain and invigorate the implementation 
process through collaboration with states, communities, civil society 
organisations, and development partners.
v
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencies, and all stakeholders 
across the country will work together to ensure the effective 
implementation of the curriculum based on the set-out strategic plan 
to accelerate the achievement of our desired result.
Dr. Tunji Maruf Alausa CON
Honourable Minister of Education
Professor Suwaiba Said Ahmad
Honourable Minister of State for Education 
vi
Education, no doubt, plays an important role as the foremost 
effective channel and instrument for providing solid bases, 
building blocks, and appropriate mechanisms for economic, 
political, social, cultural, and overall national development. The 
current reform process in the education sector, anchored on the 
Renewed Hope Agenda of the current administration, is strategic in 
the effort to place Nigeria on the right track for economic 
emancipation, human capital development, and social 
transformation. 
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives, as well as those 
contained in the global agenda, including the education 2030 agenda 
encapsulated in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there 
was the need to prioritise curriculum reform across all levels of 
education. Thus, one of the Presidential mandates for the Federal 
Ministry of Education, as exemplified in the Ministerial Deliverables, is 
to achieve a rapid review of the educational curriculum across all 
levels of education to ensure alignment with skills needed in the 
labour market. Furthermore, since the introduction of the extant 
Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) in 2011, the world 
has witnessed tremendous transformation shaped by the 
revolutionary and evolutionary force of Information Communication 
Technology (ICT) and other social forces. There have also been 
emerging and prevailing issues in health, energy, sports, values, and 
all other aspects of human existence. 
The issues highlighted above provided a basis for the review of the 
curriculum. This is further strengthened by an overriding vision to 
produce learners with functional, transferable, technological, 
vocational and entrepreneurial skills. These skills are needed for the 
country's economic development and individual fulfilment in a 
competitive globalised environment. Thus, the revision of the SSEC is 
founded on the philosophy of ensuring that every senior secondary 
school graduate is well prepared for higher education, imbued with 
relevant functional skills needed for the work, job creation and wealth 
generation; and further empowered to demonstrate ethical, moral 
and democratic values, active citizens' participation and positive 
contributions for sustained growth of the nation. 
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency-
based curriculum framework, commenced with a series of 
stakeholders' engagements, including the learners. The 
stakeholders' engagements culminated in the hosting of the National 
Stakeholders' Dialogue and High-Level Policy Committee (HLPC) 
meeting under the leadership of the Honourable Ministers of 
Education. The HLPC considered and approved a new curriculum 
structure with the benchmarks and standards that emerged from the 
stakeholders' engagements and the nationwide needs assessment 
conducted by NERDC. The new structure, which is driven by the 
Renewed Hope Agenda of Mr. President and the Ministerial Strategic 
Plan, the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI), also 
drew from the globally agreed goals. Consequently, in the new 
structure, apart from the core and compulsory subjects, there are 
now three fields of study covering Science, Humanities and Business. 
This new structure provides an opportunity for deep learning through 
a well-structured learning pathway to prepare students for future 
career opportunities of their choice. 
Broadly, the goals of the new curriculum, as derived from the new 
structure, are to:
1. Provide education that will equip the students with sound 
moral, patriotic and democratic values that will enable them to 
be well adjusted to think independently and rationally, as well 
vii
as respect the views and feelings of others in an inclusive and 
progressive society. 
2. Provide education that will equip the students with 
knowledge, skills and the right attitude to appreciate the 
dignity of labour and the beauty of nature.
3. Offer diversified curriculum contents to cater for differences in 
talents, dispositions and opportunities for positive 
contribution to society and for informed choices in vocation 
and/or higher education pursuit.
4. Empower students for self-improvement, creativity, 
innovations, and life-long learning to take up emerging 
challenges in society for better living.
5. Develop in students broad-based digital and entrepreneurial 
skills and STEM/STEAM for global competitiveness, self-
reliance, job creation and wealth generation.
6. Equip students with 21st-century skills in all spheres of 
learning to enable them to function effectively in the world of 
work and in the global community.  
7. Promote inclusiveness and interdisciplinarity in curriculum 
delivery.
Therefore, by the end of senior secondary education, all students are 
expected to: 
1. Exhibit sound moral, patriotic and democratic values in their 
day-to-day life.
2. Respect the views and feelings of others for peaceful and 
harmonious co-existence.
3. Appreciate and preserve the beauty of nature.
4.  Adopt interdisciplinary approaches in solving societal 
problems and managing personal well-being.
5. Make informed career choices that align with their life 
ambitions, talents, dispositions and available local and 
international opportunities.
6. Demonstrate excellence in day-to-day activities at school and 
in society, irrespective of abilities or disabilities.
7. Apply digital and entrepreneurial skills to create jobs and 
generate wealth.
8. Exhibit leadership qualities and democratic ideals in societal 
conduct and group dynamics
9. Apply 21st-century skills and STEM/STEAM-oriented practices 
in the learning process and in daily life activities.
10. Utilise ICT skills in all spheres of learning to function 
effectively in society and compete favourably in the global 
arena. 
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes 
and specific learning outcomes were developed with specific 
reference to the subject's unique identities and nature. The 
curriculum contents are therefore organised around the specific 
learning outcomes spread across the thematic areas. The outcomes 
place clear expectations on the teaching and learning process, with 
emphasis on what the students can do after undergoing an 
instructional period. They also inform the teachers, parents, 
examination bodies and policy makers what knowledge, skills and 
competencies the learners are expected to demonstrate at every 
given time in the instructional process. There are also competencies 
that the learners are expected to acquire and exhibit after being 
exposed to a series of learning experiences under a given topic. 
These competencies are not subject-specific but transversal and 
therefore can be acquired and applied across all topics in the 
teaching and learning process. These competencies prepare the 
learners for meaningful living in all circumstances and across 
geographical divides.
 
The New Revised Senior Secondary Education Curriculum is student-
centric and has integrated critical national and global issues as

A wide spectrum of stakeholders, including experts, subject matter 
specialists, teachers, teacher educators, policy makers, employers of 
labour, parents, development partners, private school owners and 
students participated at each of these stages. We acknowledge the 
invaluable contributions of these stakeholders. 
I acknowledge the efforts of the NERDC Staff who worked 
relentlessly to ensure the successful completion of the revision of the 
curriculum within the scheduled period.  I would like to 
posthumously acknowledge and appreciate my predecessor, the late 
Professor Ismail Junaidu, who commenced the process for 
developing the new curriculum prior to his demise in July 2024 while 
still in active service.
I extend my sincere gratitude to the Honourable Minister of

Professor Salisu Shehu

means of developing abilities and nurturing creative skills and other 
valuable skills in the learners. Furthermore, the curriculum provides 
the opportunity for the teaching and learning of emerging issues like 
Climate change, Artificial Intelligence (AI), biosafety, security, 
robotics, peace education, and blue and green education. The 
introduction of these emerging issues and other core elements of 
learning was based on the curriculum's fundamental principles of 
interdisciplinary learning, ethical and social responsibility, resilience st
and inclusivity. It also embodied aspects of the 21  Century Skills, 
including critical thinking, problem solving, information literacy and 
digital skills, communication and collaboration, global citizenship and   
cultural awareness, creativity and innovation. Moreover, it captured  
issues of entrepreneurship, environmental and sustainability 
education and financial literacy. These issues and aspects were 
covered in the curriculum based on a systematic curriculum design 
process and standards that prevented content overload.
The curriculum review process followed the established process of 
NERDC's curriculum and material development, namely:
i. Pre-design processes (including needs assessment,

ii. Planning, which involves concepts/strategy formulation,

The review of the Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) was 
undertaken in response to the overdue curriculum implementation cycle, 
expansion of disciplinary knowledge, rapid technological advancement, 
evolving policy directions, and emerging global best practices. These contextual 
and developmental imperatives exert both broad and specific influences on the 
structure, focus, and implementation of subject curricula. In particular, they affect 
the underlying philosophy, methodological approach, and the selection of 
objectives, learning outcomes, content, delivery strategies, instructional 
resources, and evaluation mechanisms.
Following the new curriculum structure, apart from the core-compulsory subjects, 
there are now three fields of study comprising Science, Humanities and Business. 
Geography constitutes one of the subjects within the Science Field of Study. The 
curriculum is designed to equip learners with foundational and advanced skills and 
competencies relevant to sciences. The curriculum is designed to achieve the 
following general objectives:
1. Build in students the foundational knowledge of geographical concepts 
and its applications
2. Equip students with ability to observe, describe and analyse physical and 
human features within the environment
3. Appreciate the earth's place in the solar system and how it influences life
4. Promote awareness of Nigeria's natural resources - their types, 
distribution and economic significance, while encouraging responsible 
attitude towards sustainable management.
5. Introduce students to modern geospatial technologies (e.g. GIS, remote 
sensing) and their application to real life situation.
The curriculum adopts a competency and outcome-based approach aimed at 
developing practical and transferable skills for productive engagement and lifelong 
learning. The competency framework clearly specifies performance expectations, 
establishes core skills benchmarks and promotes inclusivity in 
learning. It is explicitly practical and skill-oriented, and results-
driven.
Furthermore, the curriculum design follows a thematic, spiral, 
cyclical, and concentric model, in which learning content is 
systematically sequenced, reinforced, and progressively deepened 
across class levels to align with students' developmental stages and 
cognitive growth. The focus of learning is therefore on demonstrable 
competencies—on what students can do—making the curriculum 
student-centred, performative, and achievement-oriented. This 
implies that the teaching and learning process is expected to be 
active, engaging and solely focused on the development of students' 
understanding of key concepts and the appropriate demonstration of 
necessary skills and competencies. Through this, students not only 
acquire conceptual knowledge but also and importantly, acquire the 
necessary skills for functional living in society. Thus, the expectations 
on the students go beyond classroom experiences to their everyday 
lives.
Overview of the content coverage

5. Organisation of periodic capacity-building workshops for 
teachers, supervisors, and quality assurance officers to 
enhance curriculum interpretation and implementation

Effective implementation of this curriculum will generate far-reaching 
benefits for Nigeria's education system and the wider society. By 
equipping students with relevant knowledge, practical skills and core 
competencies, the curriculum will support the development of 
articulate, confident and globally competitive citizens who would 
meaningfully contribute to Nigeria's socio-economic growth and 
development.
Overall, this curriculum provides a transformative learning framework 
that transcends conventional classroom instruction to empower st
students with knowledge, skills and attitudes for daily living in the 21  
Century.

FOREWORD 
Our national education reform agenda under the Nigeria Education Sector Reform 
Initiative (NESRI) is driven by the overarching vision to improve learning outcomes 
and empower young people with knowledge, skills and competencies for national 
relevance and global competitiveness. A strategic process for achieving this is the 
overhaul of the school curriculum, as enunciated in the Renewed Hope Agenda of 
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, which identified, as a key priority area, the 
development and implementation of a modern standard curriculum for the Nigerian 
education sector. The substance of the agenda was given impetus in the Ministerial 
Deliverables for the Federal Ministry of Education, which mandates, among others, 
a rapid review of the educational curriculum across all levels of education to align 
with skills needed in the labour market. 
In our quest to achieve this lofty vision, we activated a strategic framework for the 
review, realignment and refocusing of all school curricula for functionality and 
relevance. The plan is to make our learners relevant and properly cultivated to 
contribute effectively to societal development, leveraging the right skill set. The 
above underscores the need for us to move from the knowledge-based curriculum, 
which hitherto has dominated our educational landscape, to the competency and 
outcome-based curriculum framework with a focus on developing and deepening, 
in the recipients, critical skills for efficient performance in the world of work and 
productive engagement in the ever-changing society.  
Committed to this dream, we have been able to achieve a c omplete reform of the 
basic education curriculum, aligning it to the national developmental agenda and 
global standards. Logically, the next step is the review and remodelling of the senior 
secondary education curriculum to achieve proper linkage with the basic education 
learning contents, as well as expand to learning experiences of a higher domain 
that match their cognitive maturity and societal expectations. Thus, the revised 
senior secondary education curriculum is not only competency -based but highly 
skill-oriented to produce citizens with the requisite skills for job creation and wealth 
generation. It has also fully embedded our cherished values, history and heritage 
to ensure that the learners are imbued with qualities that are fundamental for 
building a peaceful and democratic society of choice. Furthermore, the curriculum 
has been designed to expose learners to the 21st-century skills for functionality in 
all spheres of human endeavour within and outside the shores of Nigeria. These 
features make the  curriculum unique and appropriate to our current needs as a 
nation.  
We wish to state that the development of the curriculum followed various stages, 
best practices, and broadened engagement of a range of stakeholders, students, 
parents, education adminis trators, experts and professional bodies, and 
development partners. We commend the efforts of the Nigerian Educational 
Research and Development Council (NERDC) for the excellent coordination of the 
processes and technical inputs in the design of this new c urriculum. We also 
commend all the critical stakeholders, members of the academia, teachers, 
community leaders, policy makers, parents and learners who participated at 
various stages of the development process.  
We wish to reiterate our commitment to the s uccessful implementation of the 
revised curriculum through extensive teacher training and orientation, provision of 
necessary resources, and deployment of competent school quality assurance 
officers. Additionally, we will sustain and invigorate the impleme ntation process 
through collaboration with states, communities, civil society organisations, and 
development partners. 
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencies, and all stakeholders across the 
country will work together to ensure the effective implementation of the curriculum 
based on the set -out strategic plan to accelerate the achievement of our desired 
result. 
 
Dr. Tunji Maruf Alausa CON        Professor Suwaiba Said Ahmad 
Honourable Minister of Education        Honourable Minister of State for Education  
 
vi 
 
 PREFACE  
Education, no doubt, plays an important role as the foremost  effective 
channel and instrument for providing solid bases, building blocks, and 
appropriate mechanisms for economic, political, social, cultural, and overall 
national development. The current reform process in the education sector, 
anchored on the Renewed Hope Agenda of the current administration, is 
strategic in the effort to place Nigeria on the right track for economic 
emancipation, human capital development, and social transformation.  
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives, as well as those contained 
in the global agenda, including the education 2030 agenda encapsulated in 
the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there was the need to prioritise 
curriculum reform across all levels of education. Thus, one of the 
Presidential mandates for the Federal Ministry of Education, as exemplified 
in the Ministerial Deliverables, is to achieve a rapid review of the educational 
curriculum across all levels of education to ensure alignment with skills 
needed in the labour market. Furthermore, since the introduction of the 
extant Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) in 2011, the world 
has witnessed tremendous transformation shaped by the revolutionary and 
evolutionary force of Information Communication Technology (ICT) and 
other social forces. There have also been emerging and prevailing issues in 
health, energy, sports, values, and all other aspects of human existence.  
The issues highlighted above provided a basis for the review of the 
curriculum. This is further strengthened by  an overriding vision to produce 
learners with functional, transferable, technological, vocational and 
entrepreneurial skills. These skills are needed for the country ’s economic 
development and individual fulfilment in a competitive globalised 
environment. Thus, the revision of the SSEC is founded on the philosophy 
of ensuring that every senior secondary school graduate is well prepared for 
higher education, imbued with relevant functional skills needed for the work, 
job creation and wealth generation; and further empowered to demonstrate 
ethical, moral and democratic values, active citizens ’ participation and 
positive contributions for sustained growth of the nation.  
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency -based 
curriculum framework, commenced with a series of stakeholders ’ 
engagements, including the learners. The stakeholders ’ engagements 
culminated in the hosting of the National Stakeholders’ Dialogue and High-
Level Policy Committee (HLPC) meeting under the leadership of the 
Honourable Ministers of Education. The HLPC considered and approved a 
new curriculum structure with the benchmarks and standards that emerged 
from the stakeholders’ engagements and the nationwide needs assessment 
conducted by NERDC. The new structure, which is driven by the Renewed 
Hope Agenda of Mr. President and the Ministerial Strategic Plan, the Nigerian 
Education Sector Renewal Initia tive (NESRI), also drew from the globally 
agreed goals. Consequently, in the new structure, apart from the core and 
compulsory subjects, there are now three fields of study covering Science, 
Humanities and Business. This new structure provides an opportuni ty for 
deep learning through a well -structured learning pathway to prepare 
students for future career opportunities of their choice.  
Broadly, the goals of the new curriculum, as derived from the new structure, 
are to: 
1. Provide education that will equip the students with sound moral, 
patriotic and democratic values that will enable them to be well 
adjusted to think independently and rationally, as well as respect 
the views and feelings of others in an inclusive and progressive 
society.  
2. Provide education that will equip the students with knowledge, 
skills and the right attitude to appreciate the dignity of labour and 
the beauty of nature. 
 
vii 
 
3. Offer diversified curriculum contents to cater for differences in 
talents, dispositions and opportunities for positive contribution to 
society and for informed choices in vocation and/or higher 
education pursuit. 
4. Empower students for self-improvement, creativity, innovations, 
and life-long learning to take up emerging challenges in society for 
better living. 
5. Develop in students broad-based digital and entrepreneurial skills 
and STEM/STEAM for global competitiveness, self-reliance, job 
creation and wealth generation. 
6. Equip students with 21st-century skills in all spheres of learning to 
enable them to function effectively in the world of work and in the 
global community.   
7. Promote inclusiveness and interdisciplinarity in curriculum delivery. 
 
Therefore, by the end of senior secondary education, all students are 
expected to:  
1. Exhibit sound moral, patriotic and democratic values in their day-
to-day life. 
2. Respect the views and feelings of others for peaceful and 
harmonious co-existence. 
3. Appreciate and preserve the beauty of nature. 
4. Adopt interdisciplinary approaches in solving societal problems 
and managing personal well-being. 
5. Make informed career choices that align with their life ambitions, 
talents, dispositions and available local and international 
opportunities. 
6. Demonstrate excellence in day-to-day activities at school and in 
society, irrespective of abilities or disabilities. 
7. Apply digital and entrepreneurial skills to create jobs and generate 
wealth. 
8. Exhibit leadership qualities and democratic ideals in societal 
conduct and group dynamics 
9. Apply 21st-century skills and STEM/STEAM-oriented practices in the 
learning process and in daily life activities. 
10. Utilise ICT skills in all spheres of learning to function effectively in 
society and compete favourably in the global arena.  
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes and 
specific learning outcomes were develope d with specific reference to the 
subject's unique identities and nature. The curriculum contents are 
therefore organised around the specific learning outcomes spread across 
the thematic areas. The outcomes place clear expectations on the teaching 
and learn ing process, with emphasis on what the students can do after 
undergoing an instructional period. They also inform the teachers, parents, 
examination bodies and policy makers what knowledge, skills and 
competencies the learners are expected to demonstrate at every given time 
in the instructional process. There are also competencies that the learners 
are expected to acquire and exhibit after being exposed to a series of 
learning experiences under a given topic. These competencies are not 
subject-specific but transversal and therefore can be acquired and applied 
across all topics in the teaching and learning process. These competencies 
prepare the learners for meaningful living in all circumstances and across 
geographical divides.  
The New Revised Senior Secondary Education Curriculum is student-centric 
and has integrated critical national and global issues as means of developing 
abilities and nurturing creative skills and other valuable skills in the learners. 
Furthermore, the curriculum provides the opportunit y for the teaching and 
learning of emerging issues like Climate change, Artificial Intelligence (AI), 
biosafety, security, robotics, peace education, and blue and green education. 
The introduction of these emerging issues and other core elements of 
learning was based on the curriculum's fundamental principles of 
 
viii 
 
interdisciplinary learning, ethical and social responsibility, resilience and 
inclusivity. It also embodied aspects of the 21 st Century Skills, including 
critical thinking, problem solving, informat ion literacy and digital skills,  
communication and collaboration, global citizenship and cultural awareness, 
creativity and innovation. Moreover, it captured issues of entrepreneurship, 
environmental and sustainability education and financial literacy. The se 
issues and aspects were covered in the curriculum based on a systematic 
curriculum design process and standards that prevented content overload. 
The curriculum review process followed the established process of NERDC’s 
curriculum and material development, namely: 
i. Pre-design processes (including needs assessment, stakeholder 
dialogue, and setting standards) 
ii. Planning, which involves concepts/strategy formulation, 
iii. Writing/review/design, which involves the design and drafting of the 
curriculum, 
iv. Critique workshop as well as 
v. Editorial and finalisation of the curriculum documents. 
vi. Approval protocol 
A wide spectrum of stakeholders, including experts, subject matter 
specialists, teachers, teacher educators, policy makers, employers of labour, 
parents, development partners, private school owners and students 
participated at each of these stages. We acknowledge the invaluable 
contributions of these stakeholders.  
I acknowledge the efforts of the NERDC Staff who worked relentlessly to 
ensure the successful completion of the revision of the curriculum within the 
scheduled period.  I would like to posthumously acknowledge and 
appreciate my predecessor, the late Professor Ismail Junaidu, who 
commenced the process for developing the new curriculum prior to his 
demise in July 2024 while still in active service. 
I extend my sincere gratitude to the Honourable Minister of Education and 
Honourable Minister of State for Education for their invaluable support and 
visionary leadership in our endeavour to make education accessible to all 
Nigerian children, regardless of their circumstances.  
 
 
 
Professor Salisu Shehu  
Executive Secretary, NERDC 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ix 
 
INTRODUCTION  
The review of the Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) was 
undertaken in response to the overdue curriculum imp lementation cycle, 
expansion of disciplinary knowledge, rapid technological advancement, 
evolving policy directions, and emerging global best practices. These 
contextual and developmental imperatives exert both broad and specific 
influences on the structure, focus, and implementation of subject curricula. 
In particular, they affect the underlying philosophy, methodological 
approach, and the selection of objectives, learning outcomes, content, 
delivery strategies, instructional resources, and evaluation mechanisms. 
Following the new curriculum structure, apart from the core -compulsory 
subjects, there are now three fields of study comprising Science, Humanities 
and Business. Nigerian History constitutes one of the subjects within the 
Humanities Field of Study. The curriculum is designed to equip learners with 
foundational and advanced skills and competencies needed to analyse and 
appreciate Nigerian History. The curriculum is designed to achieve the 
following general objectives: 
1. To promote students’ understanding of the evolution of the Nigerian 
people and societies in order to foster a sense of pride and 
ownership in their cultural identity , democratic values and 
responsible leadership. 
2. To equip students with historical knowledge of Nigeria’s encounters 
with the outside world through trade and colonialism to appreciate 
some of the origins of Nigeria ’s contemporary problems, and draw 
lessons from them. 
3. To promote Students’ understanding of Nigeria’s achievements and 
challenges since independence, to appreciate the achievements and 
proffer solutions to the challenges. 
4. To expose students to the socio -political and economic history of 
West Africa and Africa in order to broaden their perspectives on the 
achievements and problems of the sub-continent and the continent. 
5. To expose students to the industrial revolution, world wars, global 
pandemics and climate change in world history  to enable them 
identify historical patterns, assess cause -and-effect relationships, 
and draw connections between past events and their implications. 
6. To cultivate in students an appreciation of Nigeria’s unity in diversity 
for harmonious co -existence and national development, and 
become active and responsible citizens. 
The curriculum adopts a competency and outcome -based approach aimed 
at developing practical and transferable skills for productive engagement 
and lifelong learning. The competency framework clearly specifies 
performance expectations, establishes core skills benchmarks and promotes 
inclusivity in learning. It is explicitly practical and skill-oriented, and results-
driven. 
Furthermore, the curriculum design follows a thematic, spiral, cyclical, and 
concentric model, in which learning content is systematically sequenced, 
reinforced, and progressively deepened across class levels to ali gn with 
students’ developmental stages and cognitive growth. The focus of learning 
is therefore on demonstrable competencies —on what students can do —
making the curriculum student -centred, performative, and achievement -
oriented. This implies that the teaching and learning process is expected to 
be active, engaging and solely focused on the development of students ’ 
understanding of key concepts and the appropriate demonstration of 
necessary skills and competencies. Through this, students not only acquire 
conceptual knowledge but also and importantly, acquire the necessary skills 
for functional living in society. Thus, the expectations on the students go 
beyond classroom experiences to their everyday lives.

Delivery Strategy 
The effective implementation of this curriculum requires the following: 
1. Adoption of student -centred instructional strategies that pr omote 
active engagement, collaboration, and creativity. 
2. Utilisation of diverse instructional resources, including digital tools 
and practical equipment, to enhance experiential and applied 
learning. 
3. Implementation of a lesson plan that integrates all essen tial 
elements of the new curriculum.  
4. Provision of curriculum copies to relevant teachers and school 
administrators, with emphasis on consistent and effective use. 
5. Organisation of periodic capacity -building workshops for teachers, 
supervisors, and quality assurance officers to enhance curriculum 
interpretation and implementation competence. 
6. Alignment of assessment practices with the competency and 
outcome-based framework. 
Effective implementation of this curriculum will generate far -reaching 
benefits for Nigeria’s education system and the wider society. By equipping 
students with relevant knowledge, practical skills and core competencies, 
the curriculum will support the development of articulate, confident and 
globally competitive citizens who would meaningfully contribute to Nigeria’s 
socio-economic growth and development. 
Overall, this curriculum provides a transformative learning framework that 
transcends conventional classroom instruction to empower students with 
knowledge, skills and attitudes for daily living in the 21st Century. 
 
 
Dr. Chima Jonas Egbujuo

FOREWORD 
Our national education reform agenda under the Nigeria Ed ucation Sector 
Reform Initiative (NESRI) is driven by the overarching vision to improve 
learning outcomes and empower young people with knowledge, skills and 
competencies for national relevance and global competitiveness. A strategic 
process for achieving this is the overhaul of the school curriculum, as 
enunciated in the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, 
GCFR, which identified, as a key priority area, the development and 
implementation of a modern standard curriculum for the Nigerian education 
sector. The substance of the agenda was given impetus in the Ministerial 
Deliverables for the Federal Ministry of Education, which mandates, among 
others, a rapid review of the educational curriculum across all levels of 
education to align with skills needed in the labour market. 
In our quest to achieve this lofty vision, we activated a strategic framework 
for the review, realignment and refocusing of all school curricula for 
functionality and relevance. The plan is to make our learners relevant and 
properly cultivated to contribute effectively to societal development, 
leveraging the right skill set. The above underscores the need for us to move 
from the knowledge -based curriculum, which hitherto has dominated our 
educational landscape, to the competen cy and outcome -based curriculum 
framework with a focus on developing and deepening, in the recipients, 
critical skills for efficient performance in the world of work and productive 
engagement in the ever-changing society.  
Committed to this dream, we have been able to achieve a complete reform 
of the basic education curriculum, aligning it to the national developmental 
agenda and global standards. Logically, the next step is the review and 
remodelling of the senior secondary education curriculum to achieve proper 
linkage with the basic education learning contents, as well as expand to 
learning experiences of a higher domain that match their cognitive maturity 
and societal expectations. Thus, the revised senior secondary education 
curriculum is not only competency-based but highly skill-oriented to produce 
citizens with the requisite skills for job creation and wealth generation. It 
has also fully embedded our cherished values, history and heritage to 
ensure that the learners are imbued with qualities that are fundamental for 
building a peaceful and democratic society of choice. Furthermore, the 
curriculum has been designed to expose learners to the 21st -century skills 
for functionality in all spheres of human endeavour within and outside the 
shores of Nigeria.  These features make the curriculum unique and 
appropriate to our current needs as a nation.  
We wish to state that the development of the curriculum followed various 
stages, best practices, and broadened engagement of a range of 
stakeholders, students, pa rents, education administrators, experts and 
professional bodies, and development partners. We commend the efforts of 
the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council (NERDC) for 
the excellent coordination of the processes and technical inputs in the 
design of this new curriculum. We also commend all the critical 
stakeholders, members of the academia, teachers, community leaders, 
policy makers, parents and learners who participated at various stages of 
the development process.  
We wish to reiterate  our commitment to the successful implementation of 
the revised curriculum through extensive teacher training and orientation, 
provision of necessary resources, and deployment of competent school 
quality assurance officers. Additionally, we will sustain an d invigorate the 
implementation process through collaboration with states, communities, 
civil society organisations, and development partners. 
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencies, and all stakeholders across 
the country will work together to ensure the effective implementation of the 
curriculum based on the set -out strategic plan to accelerate the 
achievement of our desired result.

PREFACE 
Education, no doubt, plays an important role as the foremost effective 
channel and instrument for providing solid bases, building blocks, and 
appropriate mechanisms for economic, political, social, cultural, and 
overall national development. The current reform process in the education 
sector, anchored on the Renewed Hope Agenda  of the current 
administration, is strategic in the effort to place Nigeria on the right track 
for economic emancipation, human capital  development, and social 
transformation.  
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives, as well as those 
contained in the global agenda, including the education 2030 agenda 
encapsulated in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there was the 
need to prioritise curriculum reform across all levels of education. Thus, 
one of the Presidential mandates for the Federal Ministry of Education, as 
exemplified in the Ministerial Deliverables, is  to achieve a rapid review of 
the educational curriculum across all levels of education to ensure 
alignment with skills needed in the labour market. Furthermore, since the 
introduction of the extant Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) 
in 2011, the world has witnessed tremendous transformation shaped by 
the revolutionary and evolutionary force of Information Communication 
Technology (ICT) and other social forces. There have also been emerging 
and prevailing issues in health, energy, sports, values, and all other 
aspects of human existence.  
The issues highlighted above provided a basis for the review of the 
curriculum. This is further strengthened by an overriding vision to produce 
learners with functional, transferable, technological, vocational and  
entrepreneurial skills. These skills are needed for the country ’s economic 
development and individual fulfilment in a competitive globalised 
environment. Thus, the revision of the SSEC is founded on the philosophy 
of ensuring that every senior secondary s chool graduate is well prepared 
for higher education, imbued with relevant functional skills needed for the 
work, job creation and wealth generation; and further empowered to 
demonstrate ethical, moral and democratic values, active citizens ’ 
participation and positive contributions for sustained growth of the nation.  
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency -based 
curriculum framework, commenced with a series of stakeholders ’ 
engagements, including the learners. The stakeholders ’ engagements 
culminated in the hosting of the National Stakeholders’ Dialogue and High-
Level Policy Committee (HLPC) meeting under the leadership of the 
Honourable Ministers of Education. The HLPC considered and approved a 
new curriculum structure with the benchma rks and standards that 
emerged from the stakeholders’ engagements and the nationwide needs 
assessment conducted by NERDC.  
The new structure, which is driven by the Renewed Hope Agenda of Mr. 
President and the Ministerial Strategic Plan, the Nigerian Education Sector 
Renewal Initiative (NESRI), also drew from the globally agreed goals. 
Consequently, in the new structure, apart from the core and compulsory 
subjects, there are now three fields of study covering Science, Humanities 
and Business. This new struc ture provides an opportunity for deep 
learning through a well -structured learning pathway to prepare students 
for future career opportunities of their choice.  
Broadly, the goals of the new curriculum, as derived from the new 
structure, are to: 
1. Provide education that will equip the students with sound moral, 
patriotic and democratic values that will enable them to be well 
adjusted to think independently and rationally, as well as respect 
the views and feelings of others in an inclusive and progressive 
society.  
2. Provide education that will equip the students with knowledge, 
skills and the right attitude to appreciate the dignity of labour 
and the beauty of nature. 
3. Offer diversified curriculum contents to cater for differences in 
talents, dispositions and opportunities for positive contribution to 
society and for informed choices in vocation and/or higher 
education pursuit. 
vi 
 
4. Empower students for self-improvement, creativity, innovations, 
and life-long learning to take up emerging challenges in society 
for better living. 
5. Develop in students broad-based digital and entrepreneurial 
skills and STEM/STEAM for global competitiveness, self-reliance, 
job creation and wealth generation. 
6. Equip students with 21st-century skills in all spheres of learning 
to enable them to function effectively in the world of work and in 
the global community.   
7. Promote inclusiveness and interdisciplinarity in curriculum 
delivery. 
Therefore, by the end of senior secondary education, all students are 
expected to:  
1. Exhibit sound moral, patriotic and democratic values in their day-
to-day life. 
2. Respect the views and feelings of others for peaceful and 
harmonious co-existence. 
3. Appreciate and preserve the beauty of nature. 
4. Adopt interdisciplinary approaches in solving societal problems 
and managing personal well-being. 
5. Make informed career choices that align with their life ambitions, 
talents, dispositions and available local and international 
opportunities. 
6. Demonstrate excellence in day-to-day activities at school and in 
society, irrespective of abilities or disabilities. 
7. Apply digital and entrepreneurial skills to create jobs and 
generate wealth. 
8. Exhibit leadership qualities and democratic ideals in societal 
conduct and group dynamics 
9. Apply 21st-century skills and STEM/STEAM -oriented practices in 
the learning process and in daily life activities. 
10. Utilise ICT skills in all spheres of learning to function effectively 
in society and compete favourably in the global arena.  
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes and 
specific learning outcomes were developed with specific reference to the 
subject's unique identities and nature. The curriculum contents are 
therefore organised around the specific learning outcomes spread across 
the thematic areas. The outcomes place clear expectations  on the 
teaching and learning process, with emphasis on what the students can 
do after undergoing an instructional period. They also inform the teachers, 
parents, examination bodies and policy makers what knowledge, skills and 
competencies the learners are  expected to demonstrate at every given 
time in the instructional process. There are also competencies that the 
learners are expected to acquire and exhibit after being exposed to a 
series of learning experiences under a given topic. These competencies 
are not subject-specific but transversal and therefore can be acquired and 
applied across all topics in the teaching and learning process. These 
competencies prepare the learners for meaningful living in all 
circumstances and across geographical divides.  
The New Revised Senior Secondary Education Curriculum is student -
centric and has integrated critical national and global issues as means of 
developing abilities and nurturing creative skills and other valuable skills 
in the learners. Furthermore, the curricul um provides the opportunity for 
the teaching and learning of emerging issues like Climate change, Artificial 
Intelligence (AI), biosafety, security, robotics, peace education, and blue 
and green education. The introduction of these emerging issues and other 
core elements of learning was based on the curriculum's fundamental 
principles of interdisciplinary learning, ethical and social responsibility, 
resilience and inclusivity. It also embodied aspects of the 21 st Century 
Skills, including critical thinking, problem solving, information literacy and 
digital skills, communication and collaboration, global citizenship and 
cultural awareness, creativity and innovation. Moreover, it captured issues 
of entrepreneurship, environmental and sustainability education a nd 
financial literacy. These issues and aspects were covered in the curriculum 
based on a systematic curriculum design process and standards that 
prevented content overload. 
vii 
 
The curriculum review process followed the established process of 
NERDC’s curriculum and material development, namely: 
i. Pre-design processes (including needs assessment, stakeholder 
dialogue, and setting standards) 
ii. Planning, which involves concepts/strategy formulation, 
iii. Writing/review/design, which involves the design and drafting of 
the curriculum, 
iv. Critique workshop as well as 
v. Editorial and finalisation of the curriculum documents. 
vi. Approval protocol 
A wide spectrum of stakeholders, including experts, subject matter 
specialists, teachers, teacher educato rs, policy makers, employers of 
labour, parents, development partners, private school owners and 
students participated at each of these stages. We acknowledge the 
invaluable contributions of these stakeholders.  
I acknowledge the efforts of the NERDC Staff who worked relentlessly to 
ensure the successful completion of the revision of the curriculum within 
the scheduled period.  I would like to posthumously acknowledge and

visionary leadership in our endeavour to make education accessible to all 
Nigerian children, regardless of their circumstances.

INTRODUCTION  
The review of the Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) was 
undertaken in response to the overdue curriculum implementation cycle, 
expansion of disciplinary knowledge, rapid technological advancement, 
evolving policy directions, and emerging global best practices. These 
contextual and developmental imperatives exert both broad and spe cific 
influences on the structure, focus, and implementation of subject 
curricula. In particular, they affect the underlying philosophy, 
methodological approach, and the selection of objectives, learning 
outcomes, content, delivery strategies, instructiona l resources, and 
evaluation mechanisms. 
Following the new curriculum structure, apart from the core -compulsory 
subjects, there are now three fields of study comprising Science, 
Humanities and Business. Citizenship and Heritage Studies (CHS) 
constitutes one of the Core and Compulsory Subjects. The curriculum is 
designed to equip learners with foundational and advanced skills and 
competencies relevant to the cultural and historical heritage, while 
appreciating Nigeria’s diversity and cultivating in students t he skills and 
attitudes needed for ethical decision -making, leadership, and community 
service. 
The curriculum is designed to achieve the following general objectives: 
1. To enable students to understand the meaning, principles, and values 
of responsible citiz enship and how these contribute to national unity, 
peace, and development. 
2. To develop in students a sense of national identity and pride in their 
cultural and historical heritage, while appreciating Nigeria ’s diversity 
and shared destiny. 
3. To equip students  with knowledge of civic rights, duties, and 
responsibilities necessary for active participation in democratic 
governance and community development. 
4. To foster respect for the rule of law, human rights, and social justice, 
promoting tolerance, cooperation, and peaceful coexistence among 
individuals and groups. 
5. To cultivate in students the skills and attitudes needed for ethical 
decision-making, leadership, and community service, thereby 
preparing them for constructive roles in society. 
The curriculum adopts a competency and outcome-based approach aimed 
at developing practical and transferable skills for productive engagement 
and lifelong learning. The competency framework clearly specifies 
performance expectations, establishes core skills benchmarks and 
promotes inclusivity in learning. It is explicitly practical and skill -oriented, 
and results-driven. 
Furthermore, the curriculum design follows a thematic, spiral, cyclical, and 
concentric model, in which learning content is systematically sequenced, 
reinforced, and progressively deepened across class levels to align with 
students’ developmental stages and cognitive growth. The focus of 
learning is therefore on demonstrable competencies —on what students 
can do —making the curriculum student -centred, performative,  and 
achievement-oriented.  
This implies that the teaching and learning process is expected to be 
active, engaging and solely focused on the development of students ’ 
understanding of key concepts and the appropriate demonstration of 
necessary skills and competencies. Through this, students not only acquire 
conceptual knowledge but also and importantly, acquire the necessary 
skills for functional living in society. Thus, the expectations on the students 
go beyond classroom experiences to their everyday lives.

Delivery Strategy 
The effective implementation of this curriculum requires the following: 
1. Adoption of student-centred instructional strategies that promote 
active engagement, collaboration, and creativity. 
2. Utilisation of diverse instructional resources, including digital tools 
and practi cal equipment, to enhance experiential and applied 
learning. 
3. Implementation of a lesson plan that integrates all essential 
elements of the new curriculum.  
4. Provision of curriculum copies to relevant teachers and school 
administrators, with emphasis on consistent and effective use. 
5. Organisation of periodic capacity -building workshops for 
teachers, supervisors, and quality assurance officers to enhance 
curriculum interpretation and implementation competence. 
6. Alignment of assessment practices with the competen cy and 
outcome-based framework. 
 
 
 
Effective implementation of this curriculum will generate far-reaching 
benefits for Nigeria ’s education system and the wider society. By 
equipping students with relevant knowledge, practical skills and core 
competencies, the curriculum will support the development of 
articulate, confident and globally competitive citizens who would 
meaningfully contribute to Nigeria ’s socio -economic growth and 
development. 
Overall, this curriculum provides a transformative learning framework 
that transcends conventional classroom instruction to empower 
students with knowledge, skills and attitudes for daily living in the 21st 
Century.

NEW REVISED SENIOR SECONDARY SCHOOL CURRICULUM 
CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS)  
SSS 1    
October, 2025

CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS)

CHRISTIAN RELIGIOUS STUDIES (CRS) 
SSS 1
ii
October, 2025
iii
iv
Our national education reform agenda under the Nigeria 
Education Sector Reform Initiative (NESRI) is driven by the 
overarching vision to improve learning outcomes and 
empower young people with knowledge, skills and competencies for 
national relevance and global competitiveness. A strategic process 
for achieving this is the overhaul of the school curriculum, as 
enunciated in the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Ahmed 
Tinubu, GCFR, which identified, as a key priority area, the 
development and implementation of a modern standard curriculum 
for the Nigerian education sector. The substance of the agenda was 
given impetus in the Ministerial Deliverables for the Federal Ministry 
of Education, which mandates, among others, a rapid review of the 
educational curriculum across all levels of education to align with 
skills needed in the labour market.
In our quest to achieve this lofty vision, we activated a strategic 
framework for the review, realignment and refocusing of all school 
curricula for functionality and relevance. The plan is to make our 
learners relevant and properly cultivated to contribute effectively to 
societal development, leveraging the right skill set. The above 
underscores the need for us to move from the knowledge-based 
curriculum, which hitherto has dominated our educational 
landscape, to the competency and outcome-based curriculum 
framework with a focus on developing and deepening, in the 
recipients, critical skills for efficient performance in the world of work 
and productive engagement in the ever-changing society. 
Committed to this dream, we have been able to achieve a complete 
reform of the basic education curriculum, aligning it to the national 
developmental agenda and global standards. Logically, the next step 
is the review and remodelling of the senior secondary education 
curriculum to achieve proper linkage with the basic education 
learning contents, as well as expand to learning experiences of a 
higher domain that match their cognitive maturity and societal 
expectations. Thus, the revised senior secondary education 
curriculum is not only competency-based but highly skill-oriented to 
produce citizens with the requisite skills for job creation and wealth 
generation. It has also fully embedded our cherished values, history 
and heritage to ensure that the learners are imbued with qualities 
that are fundamental for building a peaceful and democratic society 
of choice. Furthermore, the curriculum has been designed to expose 
learners to the 21st-century skills for functionality in all spheres of 
human endeavour within and outside the shores of Nigeria. These 
features make the curriculum unique and appropriate to our current 
needs as a nation.
 
We wish to state that the development of the curriculum followed 
various stages, best practices, and broadened engagement of a 
range of stakeholders, students, parents, education administrators, 
experts and professional bodies, and development partners. We 
commend the efforts of the Nigerian Educational Research and 
Development Council (NERDC) for the excellent coordination of the 
processes and technical inputs in the design of this new curriculum. 
We also commend all the critical stakeholders, members of the 
academia, teachers, community leaders, policy makers, parents and 
learners who participated at various stages of the development 
process.
 
We wish to reiterate our commitment to the successful 
implementation of the revised curriculum through extensive teacher 
training and orientation, provision of necessary resources, and 
v
deployment of competent school quality assurance officers. 
Additionally, we will sustain and invigorate the implementation 
process through collaboration with states, communities, civil society 
organisations, and development partners.
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencies, and all stakeholders 
across the country will work together to ensure the effective 
implementation of tcurriculum based on the set-out strategic plan to 
accelerate the achievement of our desired result.    
Dr. Tunji Maruf Alausa CON
Honourable Minister of Education 
Professor Suwaiba Said Ahmad
H       onourable Minister of State for Education
vi
Education, no doubt, plays an important role as the foremost 
effective channel and instrument for providing solid bases, 
building blocks, and appropriate mechanisms for economic, 
political, social, cultural, and overall national development. The 
current reform process in the education sector, anchored on the 
Renewed Hope Agenda of the current administration, is strategic in 
the effort to place Nigeria on the right track for economic 
emancipation, human capital development, and social 
transformation. 
To attain all the lofty values of socioeconomic development and 
reconstruction enshrined in the reform initiatives, as well as those 
contained in the global agenda, including the education 2030 agenda 
encapsulated in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there 
was the need to prioritise curriculum reform across all levels of 
education. Thus, one of the Presidential mandates for the Federal 
Ministry of Education, as exemplified in the Ministerial Deliverables, is 
to achieve a rapid review of the educational curriculum across all 
levels of education to ensure alignment with skills needed in the 
labour market. Furthermore, since the introduction of the extant 
Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) in 2011, the world 
has witnessed tremendous transformation shaped by the 
revolutionary and evolutionary force of Information Communication 
Technology (ICT) and other social forces. There have also been 
emerging and prevailing issues in health, energy, sports, values, and 
all other aspects of human existence.
 
The issues highlighted above provided a basis for the review of the 
curriculum. This is further strengthened by an overriding vision to 
produce learners with functional, transferable, technological, 
vocational and entrepreneurial skills. These skills are needed for the 
country's economic development and individual fulfilment in a 
competitive globalised environment. Thus, the revision of the SSEC is 
founded on the philosophy of ensuring that every senior secondary 
school graduate is well prepared for higher education, imbued with 
relevant functional skills needed for the work, job creation and wealth 
generation; and further empowered to demonstrate ethical, moral 
and democratic values, active citizens' participation and positive 
contributions for sustained growth of the nation. 
The review, which was anchored on the outcome and competency-
based curriculum framework, commenced with a series of 
stakeholders' engagements, including the learners. The 
stakeholders' engagements culminated in the hosting of the National 
Stakeholders' Dialogue and High-Level Policy Committee (HLPC) 
meeting under the leadership of the Honourable Ministers of 
Education. The HLPC considered and approved a new curriculum 
structure with the benchmarks and standards that emerged from the 
stakeholders' engagements and the nationwide needs assessment 
conducted by NERDC. The new structure, which is driven by the 
Renewed Hope Agenda of Mr. President and the Ministerial Strategic 
Plan, the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI), also 
drew from the globally agreed goals. Consequently, in the new 
structure, apart from the core and compulsory subjects, there are 
now three fields of study covering Science, Humanities and Business. 
This new structure provides an opportunity for deep learning through 
a well-structured learning pathway to prepare students for future 
career opportunities of their choice. 
Broadly, the goals of the new curriculum, as derived from the new 
structure, are to:
1. Provide education that will equip the students with sound 
moral, patriotic and democratic values that will enable them 
to be well adjusted to think independently and rationally, as 
well as respect the views and feelings of others in an 
vii
inclusive and progressive society.
2. Provide education that will equip the students with 
knowledge, skills and the right attitude to appreciate the 
dignity of labour and the beauty of nature.
3. Offer diversified curriculum contents to cater for differences 
in talents, dispositions and opportunities for positive 
contribution to society and for informed choices in vocation 
and/or higher education pursuit.
4. Empower students for self-improvement, creativity, 
innovations, and life-long learning to take up emerging 
challenges in society for better living.
5. Develop in students broad-based digital and entrepreneurial 
skills and STEM/STEAM for global competitiveness, self-
reliance, job creation and wealth generation.
6. Equip students with 21st-century skills in all spheres of 
learning to enable them to function effectively in the world 
of work and in the global community.  
7. Promote inclusiveness and interdisciplinarity in curriculum 
delivery.
Therefore, by the end of senior secondary education, all students are 
expected to: 
1. Exhibit sound moral, patriotic and democratic values in their 
day-to-day life.
2. Respect the views and feelings of others for peaceful and 
harmonious co-existence.
3. Appreciate and preserve the beauty of nature.
4. Adopt interdisciplinary approaches 
in solving societal problems and managing personal well-
being.
5. Make informed career choices that align with their life 
ambitions, talents, dispositions and available local and 
international opportunities.
6. Demonstrate excellence in day-to-day activities at school 
and in society, irrespective of abilities or disabilities.
7. Apply digital and entrepreneurial skills to create jobs and 
generate wealth.
8. Exhibit leadership qualities and democratic ideals in societal 
conduct and group dynamics
9. Apply 21st-century skills and STEM/STEAM-oriented practices 
in the learning process and in daily life activities.
10. Utilise ICT skills in all spheres of learning to function 
effectively in society and compete favourably in the global 
arena. 
These generic outcomes provided the basis upon which the themes 
and specific learning outcomes were developed with specific 
reference to the subject's unique identities and nature. The 
curriculum contents are therefore organised around the specific 
learning outcomes spread across the thematic areas. The outcomes 
place clear expectations on the teaching and learning process, with 
emphasis on what the students can do after undergoing an 
instructional period. They also inform the teachers, parents, 
examination bodies and policy makers what knowledge, skills and 
competencies the learners are expected to demonstrate at every 
given time in the instructional process. There are also competencies 
that the learners are expected to acquire and exhibit after being 
exposed to a series of learning experiences under a given topic. 
These competencies are not subject-specific but transversal and 
therefore can be acquired and applied across all topics in the 
teaching and learning process. These competencies prepare the 
learners for meaningful living in all circumstances and across 
geographical divides. 
The New Revised Senior Secondary Education Curriculum is student-
centric and has integrated critical national and global issues as 
means of developing abilities and nurturing creative skills and other 
viii
valuable skills in the learners. Furthermore, the curriculum provides 
the opportunity for the teaching and learning of emerging issues like 
Climate change, Artificial Intelligence (AI), biosafety, security, 
robotics, peace education, and blue and green education. The 
introduction of these emerging issues and other core elements of 
learning was based on the curriculum's fundamental principles of 
interdisciplinary learning, ethical and social responsibility, resilience st
and inclusivity. It also embodied aspects of the 21  Century Skills, 
including critical thinking, problem solving, information literacy and 
digital skills, communication and collaboration, global citizenship and   
cultural awareness, creativity and innovation. Moreover, it captured  
issues of entrepreneurship, environmental and sustainability 
education and financial literacy. These issues and aspects were 
covered in the curriculum based on a systematic curriculum design 
process and standards that prevented content overload.
The curriculum review process followed the established process of 
NERDC's curriculum and material development, namely:
i. Pre-design processes (including needs assessment, 
stakeholder dialogue, and setting standards)
ii. Planning, which involves concepts/strategy formulation,
iii. Writing/review/design, which involves the design and drafting 
of the curriculum,
iv. Critique workshop as well as
v. Editorial and finalisation of the curriculum documents.
vi. Approval protocol
A wide spectrum of stakeholders, including experts, subject matter 
specialists, teachers, teacher educators, policy makers, employers of 
labour, parents, development partners, private school owners and 
students participated at each of these stages. We acknowledge the 
invaluable contributions of these stakeholders. 
I acknowledge the efforts of the NERDC Staff who worked relentlessly 
to ensure the successful completion of the revision of the curriculum 
within the scheduled period.  I would like to posthumously 
acknowledge and appreciate my predecessor, the late Professor 
Ismail Junaidu, who commenced the process for developing the new 
curriculum prior to his demise in July 2024 while still in active service.
I extend my sincere gratitude to the Honourable Minister of Education 
and Honourable Minister of State for Education for their invaluable 
support and visionary leadership in our endeavour to make education 
accessible to all Nigerian children, regardless of their circumstances. 
Professor Salisu Shehu 
Executive Secretary, NERDC 
he review of the Senior Secondary Education Curriculum (SSEC) was 
Tundertaken in response to the overdue curriculum implementation cycle, 
expansion of disciplinary knowledge, rapid technological advancement, 
evolving policy directions, and emerging global best practices. These contextual 
and developmental imperatives exert both broad and specific influences on the 
structure, focus, and implementation of subject curricula. In particular, they affect 
the underlying philosophy, methodological approach, and the selection of 
objectives, learning outcomes, content, delivery strategies, instructional 
resources, and evaluation mechanisms.
Following the new curriculum structure, apart from the core-compulsory subjects, 
there are now three fields of study comprising Science, Humanities and Business. 
Christian Religious Studies constitutes one of the subjects within the Humanities 
Field of Study. The curriculum is designed to equip learners with foundational and 
advanced skills and competencies relevant to the Christian faith. The curriculum is 
designed to achieve the following general objectives:
1. Provide an opportunity for students to learn God's truth for transforming 
lives. Deuteronomy 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:2.
2. Enable students to accept Jesus Christ as their role model and be able to 
apply His life and teachings in their daily lives.
3. Expose the students to the knowledge, works, and guidance of the Holy 
Spirit.
4. Develop in the students' Christian attitudes, moral values, and religious 
tolerance for peaceful co-existence.
5. Equip the students with 21st-century skills for higher education and 
relevant careers in Christian Religious Studies.
The curriculum adopts a competency and outcome-based approach aimed at 
developing practical and transferable skills for productive engagement and lifelong 
learning. The competency framework clearly specifies performance expectations, 
establishes core skills benchmarks and promotes inclusivity in learning. It is 
explicitly practical and skill-oriented, and results-driven.
Furthermore, the curriculum design follows a thematic, spiral, cyclical, and 
concentric model, in which learning content is systematically sequenced, 
reinforced, and progressively deepened across class levels to align with students' 
developmental stages and cognitive growth. The focus of learning is therefore on 
demonstrable competencies—on what students can do—making the curriculum 
student-centred, performative, and achievement-oriented. This 
implies that the teaching and learning process is expected to be 
active, engaging and solely focused on the development of students' 
understanding of key concepts and the appropriate demonstration of 
necessary skills and competencies. Through this, students not only 
acquire conceptual knowledge but also and importantly, acquire the 
necessary skills for functional living in society. Thus, the expectations 
on the students go beyond classroom experiences to their everyday 
lives.

Foreword 
Our national education reform agenda under the Nigeria Education  Sector 
Reform Initiative (NESRI) is driven by the overarching vision to improve 
learning outcomes and empower young people with knowledge, skills and 
competencies for national relevance and global competitiveness. A strategic 
process for achieving this is the overhaul of the school curriculum , as 
enunciated in the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, 
GCFR, which identified, as a key priorit y area, the development and 
implementation of a modern standard curriculum for the Nigerian education 
sector. The substance of the agenda was given impetus in the Ministerial 
Deliverables for the Federal Ministry of Education, which mandates, among 
others, a rapid review of the educational curriculum across all levels of 
education to align with skills needed in the labour market. 
In our quest to achieve this lofty vision, we activated a strategic framework 
for the review, realignment and refocusing of all s chool curricula for 
functionality and relevance. The plan is to make our learners relevant and 
properly cultivated to contribute effectively to societal development , 
leveraging the right skill set. The above underscores the need for us to move 
from the kno wledge-based curriculum, which hitherto has dominated our 
educational landscape, to the competency and outcome -based curriculum 
framework with a focus on developing and deepening, in the recipients, 
critical skills for efficient performance in the world of  work and productive 
engagement in the ever-changing society.  
Committed to this dream, we have been able to achieve a complete reform 
of the basic education curriculum, aligning it to the national developmental 
agenda and global standards. Logically, the next step is the review and 
remodelling of the senior secondary education curriculum to achieve proper 
linkage with the basic education learning contents , as well as expand to 
learning experiences of a higher domain that match their cognitive maturity 
and societal expectations. Thus, the revised senior secondary education 
curriculum is not only competency-based but highly skill-oriented to produce 
citizens with the requisite skills for job creation and wealth generation. It 
has also fully embedded our cheri shed values, history and heritage to 
ensure that the learners are imbued with qualities that are fundamental for 
building a peaceful and democratic society of choice. Furthermore, the 
curriculum has been designed to expose learners to the 21st-century skills 
for functionality in all spheres of human endeavour within and outside the 
shores of Nigeria. These features make the curriculum unique and 
appropriate to our current needs as a nation.  
We wish to state that the development of the curriculum followed v arious 
stages, best practices, and broadened engagement of a range of 
stakeholders, students, parents, education administrators, experts and 
professional bodies, and development partners. We commend the efforts of 
the Nigerian Educational Research and Deve lopment Council (NERDC) for 
the excellent coordination of the processes and technical inputs in the 
design of this new curriculum. We also commend all the critical 
stakeholders, members of the academia, teachers, community leaders, 
policy makers, parents a nd learners who participated at various stages of 
the development process.  
We wish to reiterate our commitment to the successful implementation of 
the revised curriculum through extensive teacher training and orientation, 
provision of necessary resources,  and deployment of competent school 
quality assurance officers. Additionally, we will sustain and invigorate the 
implementation process through collaboration with states, communities, 
civil society organisations, and development partners. 
It is our hope that the States, relevant agencies, and all stakeholders across 
the country will work together to ensure the effective implementation of the 
curriculum based on the set -out strategic plan to accelerate the 
achievement of our desired result.
